KEY MESSAGE 1... 

Surface high pressure remains positioned over Nova Scotia today
with weak troughing building into the Northeast today from the
Great Lakes. Temperatures and dew points will be very similar to
yesterday with morning sun mixing with afternoon clouds as we
reach our convective temperatures. The insolation combined with
dew points in the upper 50s to around 60 and cooling 
temperatures aloft under the incoming trough will help generate 
weak instability; however, the latest HREF continues to a low 
chance (under 30-40%) for MU CAPE to exceed 1000 J/kg late this
afternoon favored in the higher terrain areas. Given weak
forcing and very weak shear aloft (15kts or less), expecting
pulse-type isolated to widely scattered convection favored in 
the southwest Adirondacks, northern/eastern Catskills, southern 
Greens, and Taconics that will be short-lived as downdrafts from
any showers/storms quickly choke off updrafts. While PWATs over
1" can support brief heavy downpours, the brief duration and 
very weak shear will mitigate any flooding or severe weather 
concerns.

Most showers/storms will be diurnally driven and diminish with 
the loss of daytime heating; however, a few isolated showers 
may lingering overnight as shown in the latest CAMs. The weak 
trough from today slides into New England tomorrow but CAMs 
still suggest another day with pulse-type and diurnally driven 
convection given westerly flow aloft advecting a slightly 
warmer/more humid air mass into the region resulting in slightly
higher instability (30 to 60% chance for at least 1000 J/kg of 
SB CAPE). Lapse rates are still weak (under 6C/km) under broad
troughing aloft but CAMs show greater coverage of diurnally 
driven pulse-type isolated to scattered convection, again 
favored in the higher terrain areas. Weak shear will mitigate 
any flooding/severe concerns but there is a low to moderate 
chance for brief downpours within any storm.

KEY MESSAGE 2...

There is moderate to high confidence in a coastal low 
developing off the NJ/southern New England coast for Tuesday 
into Wednesday resulting in periods of widespread rain tracking
into eastern NY and western New England. The guidance over the 
last two model cycles has come into better agreement with the EC
converging towards to the GFS/CMC solution which have shown 
strong upper level divergence ahead of an amplifying parent 
shortwave from the Great Lakes resulting in a coastal low south 
of Long Island. However, there remains uncertainty in how 
quickly the parent trough closes off aloft which will determine 
how far north the ensuing coastal low forms. The EC remains the 
most aggressive with the parent trough closing off the earliest 
resulting in the coastal low developing further north closer to 
NYC/Long Island. This would allow the stratiform rain band 
within the deformation zone on the north side of the low to 
track well into eastern NY and western New England. However, the
GFS and CMC are slightly delayed in the parent trough 
maturing/closing off allowing the coastal to form further south 
off the NJ coast, keeping the heaviest rain mainly south of 
I-90.

The exact track of the low will determine where the heaviest 
rainfall amounts occurr and greatest chance for flooding concern but
the increasing agreement on the overall synoptic evolution 
gives us more confidence in messaging a stratiform, moderate 
rain event. There is good agreement in the warm conveyor belt 
taping into Gulf and western Atlantic moisture with PWATs 
nearing 2" wrapping into the low as it pivots/slows down on 
Wednesday. The moderate rainfall within the deformation zone 
(and eventual TROWAL) likely also pivots as the sfc low deepens 
and matures heading into coastal New England. This raises 
concerns for isolated to scattered flash flooding as this region
can favor efficient, warm rain processes producing heavy 
rainfall rates. Latest flash flood guidance shows it will take 
more than 2 to 3" of rain within 3 hours to raise flash flooding
concerns thanks to dry antecedent conditions but a pivoting 
band within a moisture rich environment with weak instability 
raises some concerns. WPC maintains its slight risk in the 
latest Day 3/4 Excessive Rainfall Outlook focused in western New
England and areas mainly south of I-90 where the highest 
probabilities for greater than 2" of rain (40-50%) within the 
24hr period between 8PM Tues and 8PM Wed exist. Easterly winds 
up to 850hPa shows there will likely be terrain enhancement in 
the eastern Catskills and eastern slopes of the southern 
Greens/Berkshires/Taconics where the highest probabilities are 
for exceeding 2" in 24 hrs. There may even be some downsloping 
impacts on the west side of the Taconics into portions of the 
Capital District leading to lower rainfall amounts. Given the
